{"differential_diagnosis": [{"diagnosis": "Chronic allergic contact dermatitis", "confidence": 0.85}, {"diagnosis": "Nummular eczema", "confidence": 0.78}, {"diagnosis": "Lichen simplex chronicus", "confidence": 0.72}, {"diagnosis": "Psoriasis (plaque or inverse variant involving flexural/upper extremity skin)", "confidence": 0.65}, {"diagnosis": "Mycosis fungoides (early patch stage)", "confidence": 0.42}], "diagnostic_uncertainty": 1.524, "reasoning": "The key features are bilateral, chronic (5-month), pruritic, non-resolving arm rash — strongly suggesting a T-cell–mediated or immune-dysregulated inflammatory dermatosis. Chronic allergic contact dermatitis is top consideration given symmetry, chronicity, and itch; common allergens include nickel (watches, jewelry), fragrances, or topical antibiotics. Nummular eczema fits well with persistent, coin-shaped, intensely pruritic plaques on extensor arms and chronic waxing/waning course. Lichen simplex chronicus is highly plausible due to chronic itch-scratch cycle leading to lichenified, hyperpigmented, symmetric plaques — though typically more localized, it can involve both arms. Psoriasis is less typical for isolated bilateral arm involvement without classic scalp/nail/knee/elbow involvement, but flexural or atypical plaque variants do occur and may be underrecognized. Mycosis fungoides is low-probability but must be considered in any chronic, treatment-refractory, asymmetric or symmetric pruritic rash — especially if patches are hypopigmented, scaly, or show subtle epidermal atrophy; however, 5-month duration is relatively short for MF, and bilateral symmetry makes it less likely than inflammatory etiologies. No data yet on morphology, distribution (flexor vs. extensor), scale, lichenification, or triggers — limiting specificity and increasing diagnostic uncertainty."}

{"differential_diagnosis": [{"diagnosis": "Chronic spontaneous urticaria", "confidence": 0.82}, {"diagnosis": "Atopic dermatitis (chronic lichenified phase)", "confidence": 0.78}, {"diagnosis": "Lichen simplex chronicus", "confidence": 0.75}, {"diagnosis": "Nummular eczema", "confidence": 0.68}, {"diagnosis": "Mycosis fungoides (patch stage)", "confidence": 0.54}], "diagnostic_uncertainty": 1.602, "reasoning": "The 5-month duration of persistent, bilateral, itchy arm rash without clear external triggers strongly favors chronic inflammatory or immune-mediated conditions over acute contact dermatitis (which is ruled out by negative history of new exposures and lack of site-specific reproducibility). Chronic spontaneous urticaria is top consideration given the prominent pruritus and chronicity—though typical wheals may have evolved into subtle erythematous or slightly edematous patches in long-standing cases. Atopic dermatitis remains highly plausible, especially if lichenification or flexural involvement is present but unreported; its chronic relapsing course fits well. Lichen simplex chronicus is likely secondary to chronic scratching, explaining symmetry (habitual bilateral rubbing) and persistence—but requires confirmation of lichenified plaques. Nummular eczema commonly affects extensor arms, is intensely pruritic, and persists for months, though often more discrete and coin-shaped. Mycosis fungoides enters the differential due to chronic, treatment-refractory, symmetrical patch-stage disease mimicking eczema—especially given the 5-month duration and absence of trigger—yet remains less likely without additional features (e.g., scale variation, folliculocentricity, or progression), warranting biopsy only if refractory or atypical."}

{"differential_diagnosis": [{"diagnosis": "Chronic Idiopathic Urticaria", "confidence": 0.82}, {"diagnosis": "Atopic Dermatitis (Adult-Onset, Lichenified)", "confidence": 0.78}, {"diagnosis": "Lichen Simplex Chronicus", "confidence": 0.75}, {"diagnosis": "Nummular Eczema", "confidence": 0.68}, {"diagnosis": "Mycosis Fungoides (Patch Stage)", "confidence": 0.62}], "diagnostic_uncertainty": 1.609, "reasoning": "The chronic (5-month), bilateral, pruritic, non-resolving upper extremity rash without clear external trigger or scaling/crusting points away from contact dermatitis (ruled out by negative exposure history) and acute inflammatory conditions like insect bite reactions or drug eruptions. Chronic idiopathic urticaria is highly plausible given persistent pruritus and waxing/waning course—though typically with evanescent wheals, subtle or fixed variants (e.g., delayed pressure or dermographism) can mimic persistent plaques. Adult-onset atopic dermatitis often presents with lichenified, symmetric, pruritic patches on extensor surfaces (e.g., arms), especially without prominent scaling early on. Lichen simplex chronicus fits the chronic itch-scratch cycle leading to thickened, hyperpigmented, but not necessarily scaly plaques—common on accessible sites like arms. Nummular eczema is less likely due to absence of classic coin-shaped, scaly, crusted lesions, but chronic non-specific variants exist. Mycosis fungoides is lower-probability but must be considered in chronic, treatment-refractory, asymmetric or evolving patches—especially given its frequent initial misdiagnosis as eczema; absence of scale does not exclude early patch-stage disease. Confidence scores reflect clinical probability weighted by duration, symmetry, pruritus dominance, lack of triggers, and absence of overt scaling/crusting."}
